details:
**The Rite of Spring (Le Sacre du printemps)**
Stravinsky's most famous ballet, subtitled "Pictures from Pagan Russia," written for Sergei Diaghilev's Ballets Russes with choreography by Vaslav Nijinsky. Its savage rhythms, dissonance, and provocative choreography sparked a near-riot at its 1913 Paris premiere. It is divided into two parts, "The Adoration of the Earth" and "The Sacrifice."

**Opening high bassoon solo**
The Rite of Spring begins with a solo bassoon playing in an unusually high register, starting on a long C followed by B, G, E, B, and a long A. The melody is based on a Lithuanian folk song, and Stravinsky likened the introduction's woodwinds to a swarm of spring pipes.

**"Sacrificial Dance" and the Chosen One**
The finale of The Rite of Spring, in which a young girl chosen in the "Glorification of the Chosen One" dances herself to death to appease the god of spring. Its meter changes almost every measure. Other Part II sections include "Mystic Circles of the Young Girls" and "Evocation of the Ancestors."

**"Augurs of Spring" polychord**
In the Rite's "Augurs of Spring," the strings pound out a harsh repeated chord combining an F-flat major triad with an E-flat dominant seventh, with irregular accents mirrored by the stomping dancers. Part I also includes the "Procession of the Sage" (Wise Elder) and "The Kiss of the Earth."

**The Firebird and Koschei's egg**
Stravinsky's first ballet for Diaghilev (1910), based on Russian folklore. Prince Ivan enters the garden of the sorcerer Koschei (Kashchei) the Immortal, captures the magical Firebird, and with her help destroys Koschei by smashing the egg that holds his soul.

**"Infernal Dance"**
The violent dance in The Firebird, introduced by a timpani stroke, in which the Firebird bewitches Koschei and his monsters into dancing until they collapse from exhaustion.

**Berceuse and 7/4 Finale**
After the "Infernal Dance," the Firebird lulls the monsters to sleep with a Berceuse (lullaby) featuring a famous bassoon solo over harp and strings. The ballet's finale grows from a quiet horn melody into a grand ending that switches from 3/2 to 7/4 time.

**Thirteen princesses and the golden apples**
In The Firebird, thirteen princesses held captive by Koschei, led by the Tsarevna, play a game with golden apples and dance a khorovod (Russian round dance) before Ivan falls in love with one of them.

**Petrushka chord**
A bitonal chord superimposing C major and F-sharp major triads, a tritone apart, first introduced by two clarinets. It represents the title puppet whenever he appears in Petrushka and is one of the most famous chords in 20th-century music.

**Petrushka**
Stravinsky's 1911 ballet about a straw puppet who comes to life at the Shrovetide Fair in St. Petersburg. Petrushka loves the Ballerina but is trapped in his cell and finally killed by the Moor; one fair scene includes the "Wet-Nurses' Dance."

**Symphony of Psalms**
A 1930 neoclassical choral symphony written for the 50th anniversary of the Boston Symphony Orchestra. It sets three biblical psalms (including "Expectans expectavi Dominum" from Psalm 40), omits violins, violas, and clarinets, and opens with a distinctively voiced E minor chord.

**Pulcinella**
A 1920 ballet based on music attributed to Pergolesi (some actually by other 18th-century composers), often seen as the start of Stravinsky's neoclassical period. He later arranged parts of it as the Suite italienne; other neoclassical works include the Dumbarton Oaks Concerto, written for Robert and Mildred Bliss's 30th wedding anniversary, and the ballet Orpheus.

**Agon**
A plotless ballet for twelve dancers choreographed by George Balanchine, marking Stravinsky's move toward serialism. It includes a sarabande, galliard, and branles inspired by a 17th-century French court dance manual, and completes his "Greek trilogy" with Apollon musagète and Orpheus.

**The Rake's Progress**
Stravinsky's English-language opera based on William Hogarth's series of paintings and engravings, with a libretto by W. H. Auden and Chester Kallman. It follows Tom Rakewell, who abandons his beloved Anne Trulove and is led to ruin by the devilish Nick Shadow.

**Violin Concerto and the "passport chord"**
Stravinsky's Violin Concerto in D, written with violinist Samuel Dushkin, begins every movement with a triple-stop chord spanning more than two octaves. Stravinsky sketched it on a napkin; Dushkin first thought it unplayable, then found it possible, and Stravinsky called it the "passport" to the concerto.
